6.02.t: Pelvic Ring — SI Joint, Symphysis & Sciatic Foramina
6.02.b:
### SI joint & its ligaments
- SI joint → front-lower part **synovial** (auricular surface) · back-upper part **fibrous** (iliac tuberosity) (Handbook)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.5 · 6.02
- **Interosseous SI ligament** → **vertical** stability · **posterior SI** → very strong · **anterior SI** → thin, torn first in open book (Handbook)

PITFALL — strongest SI ligament
- Netter → **posterior** SI · SI anatomy notes → **interosseous** ("strongest in the body")
- Say → "**the posterior complex — interosseous and posterior SI — is the strongest**"

- **Iliolumbar** → L5 transverse process → iliac crest → **rotational** stability (Handbook)
- L5 transverse process avulsion → iliolumbar pulled → think **vertical instability**

| Fibre direction | Stability | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Horizontal** | Rotational (stops opening) | Anterior SI, iliolumbar, **sacrospinous** |
| **Vertical** | Vertical (stops upward shift) | Interosseous, **sacrotuberous** |
| **Front–back** | AP (anteroposterior) translation | Interosseous |

(Handbook)

### Greater & lesser sciatic foramina
- **Sacrospinous** (sacrum → ischial spine) + **sacrotuberous** (sacrum → ischial tuberosity) → turn the notches into 2 foramina (Handbook)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.6, 6.7 · 6.02
- **Piriformis** → fills the greater foramen → structures named **above** or **below** it

| Greater foramen — above piriformis | Greater foramen — below piriformis | Lesser foramen |
|---|---|---|
| **Superior gluteal** nerve + vessels | **Sciatic** nerve, **inferior gluteal** nerve + vessels | **Obturator internus tendon** |
| — | **Posterior femoral cutaneous** nerve, nerve to **quadratus femoris** | **Pudendal** nerve, **internal pudendal** vessels |
| — | **Pudendal** nerve, **internal pudendal** vessels, nerve to **obturator internus** | Nerve to **obturator internus** |

(Netter)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "contents of the greater and lesser sciatic foramina" (Nagah p41)
- Boundaries → greater notch + **sacrospinous** ligament; lesser notch + sacrospinous + **sacrotuberous**
- **Above piriformis** → superior gluteal nerve and vessels only
- **Below piriformis** → sciatic, inferior gluteal nerve + vessels, posterior femoral cutaneous, nerve to quadratus femoris, pudendal + internal pudendal, nerve to obturator internus
- **Greater → lesser** → **PIN** (pudendal, internal pudendal, nerve to obturator internus) hook round the ischial spine/sacrospinous
- **Lesser out** → obturator internus tendon

### Symphysis & ring stability
- **Symphysis pubis** → midline **cartilaginous** joint · superior + **arcuate (inferior)** pubic ligaments · normal width ≈**5 mm** (Handbook)

- **Diastasis ≤2.5 cm** → symphysis ligaments only · **>2.5 cm** → sacrospinous + anterior SI torn = **open book** (Handbook)
- Rule → the wider the gap, the more ligament groups are gone, front → floor → back (Handbook)

- Shear → skin and fat **degloved off the fascia** → blood and lymph collect under it (Handbook)
- Skin loses its blood supply → treat like an **open injury** → debridement (Handbook)
- Always check for **rectal or vaginal bleeding** → open pelvic fracture (Handbook)

### Neck–shaft angle, anteversion, offset
- **Neck–shaft angle** → >150° at birth → ≈140° at 5 y → **≈130° (±5°)** adult · **coxa vara <120°** (Handbook)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.17, 6.18 · 6.04

- Offset too small → greater trochanter impinges + unstable · too big → ITB (iliotibial band) rubs the trochanteric bursa → lateral pain (Gobba)

PITFALL — "normal" anteversion
- Ultrasound → women 18°, men 14° (Bråten 1992) · CT of normal femurs → mean ≈9°, retroversion common (Koerner 2013)
- Say → "**about 10–15°, a little more in women**" → measure the other side before nailing
- Measure (Prof Ibrahim Nassar, Nagah p3) → **Craig test** · X-ray · **CT scanogram** · ultrasound
  - Craig → prone, knee 90°, trochanter most lateral → leg angle = femoral, not acetabular, version

### Calcar, trabeculae & Ward triangle
- **Calcar femorale** → vertical plate of dense bone, **posteromedial** neck–shaft junction → carries load from neck cortex to shaft cortex (Netter; Handbook)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.19, 6.20 · 6.04

| Trabecular group (Netter) | Runs |
|---|---|
| **Primary compressive** | Top of the head → medial neck → strongest |
| **Primary tensile** | Lower head → lateral cortex below the greater trochanter |
| Secondary compressive / tensile | Along stress lines lower down |
| Greater trochanter group | Inside the trochanter |
| **Ward triangle** | Empty zone between them in the neck |

- Wolff's law → trabeculae follow stress lines → they fade in order in osteoporosis (Netter)

- Triangles → **Ward** = osteoporosis · **Fairbank** = coxa vara · **Babcock** = TB (tuberculosis)

- Neck fracture → **intracapsular** → slight ER (external rotation) · intertrochanteric → **extracapsular** → **marked ER**, foot flat on the table

6.05.b:
### Why the femur bows forward
- Shaft → tube with an **anterior bow**; concave side behind (Netter)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.21 · 6.05
- Radius of the bow ≈**1 m** (≈1,030 mm); most nails are straighter (>1,300 mm) → **anterior cortex** hit at the tip (Mittal 2023)

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "why is the femur curved anteriorly?" (Nagah p40)
- Brings the knee under the **centre of gravity** of the trunk (Nagah)
- Gives room and leverage to the big **antigravity muscles** — quadriceps in front, hamstrings and adductors behind (Nagah)
- Body weight bends it predictably → **posterior concave side** under compression → thickened by the **linea aspera**

6.07.t: Blood Supply of the Femoral Head & Anastomoses
6.07.b:
### The chain — from profunda to the dome
1) **Profunda femoris** → **MFCA** (medial femoral circumflex artery, posterior) + **LFCA** (lateral femoral circumflex artery, anterior) (Netter)
[[FIG: Fig 6.27, 6.28 · 6.07
2) → **extracapsular ring** at the base of the neck
3) → **ascending cervical (retinacular) arteries** under the synovium along the neck
4) → **subsynovial ring** at the edge of the head
5) → **epiphyseal arteries** → the **lateral epiphyseal** (from the MFCA, posterosuperior) feeds the **weight-bearing dome** (Netter; Handbook)

- **Artery of ligamentum teres** (obturator) → small medial area near the fovea in adults (Netter)
- LFCA → mainly the **anterior neck** + greater trochanter in adults (Netter)

CLINICAL PEARL — why the displaced neck fracture fails
- Retinacular vessels run **inside the capsule on the posterosuperior neck** → a displaced neck fracture tears them (Netter; Nagah p12)
- Result → **AVN** (avascular necrosis) + **nonunion** · intertrochanteric = extracapsular, cancellous, well fed → heals (Netter)
- Dislocation → AVN 10% if reduced <6 h, 20% after (Handbook)

### MFCA deep branch — the surgeon's artery
- Runs between **pectineus and iliopsoas** → behind the neck **under quadratus femoris** (Netter)
  [[FIG: Fig 6.29, 6.30 · 6.07
- Crosses **behind obturator externus** → then **in front of the conjoint tendon** (gemelli + obturator internus) (Gautier 2000)
- Pierces the capsule at **gemellus superior** → 2–4 retinacular vessels on the **posterosuperior neck** · **obturator externus protects it** in any dislocation (Gautier 2000)
- Trochanteric branch at the upper border of quadratus femoris → marks obturator externus (Gautier 2000)

CLINICAL PEARL — saving the MFCA
- Posterior approach → cut the rotators **off the bone**, keep **obturator externus** intact (Gautier 2000)
- Back-up → **inferior gluteal artery** joins the MFCA via the piriformis branch (Zlotorowicz 2011; Grose 2008)
- Medial approach in DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip) → MFCA crosses near iliopsoas → **AVN** risk (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Neck fracture fixed in **too much valgus** → stretches the MFCA → AVN (Nagah p12)

### Supply by age
| Age | Main supply (Netter) |
|---|---|
| **0–4 y** | MFCA + LFCA + ligamentum teres artery · metaphyseal vessels still cross |
| **4–8 y** | **MFCA almost alone** → physis blocks metaphyseal vessels · ligamentum teres not yet working |
| **>8 y** | MFCA predominant · ligamentum teres adds a little |

[[FIG: Fig 6.31 · 6.07

- 4–8 y window → **peak Perthes risk** · femoral head = 75% of all osteonecrosis, bilateral in 75–80% (Handbook)
- Once the physis forms → no vessel crosses it → ischaemia kills the bony nucleus; cartilage lives on synovial fluid (Prof Abdel-Ghani)

PITFALL — ligamentum teres artery after 8 years
- Handbook → contributes **after 8 y** · Netter → "minimal supply to the adult head"
- Say → "**it helps a little after about 8 years, never enough to save the head after a displaced neck fracture**"

### Trochanteric & cruciate anastomoses
| Anastomosis | Where | Vessels |
|---|---|---|
| **Trochanteric** | Trochanteric fossa | Superior gluteal (descending) · inferior gluteal · ascending branches of MFCA + LFCA |
| **Cruciate** | Behind the femur at the **lesser trochanter**, under quadratus femoris | **Inferior gluteal** (above) · **1st perforator** (below) · transverse branches of **MFCA** (medial) + **LFCA** (lateral) |

[[FIG: Fig 6.32, 6.33 · 6.07

- Value → **internal iliac ↔ femoral system** bypass if the femoral artery is blocked above the profunda
